summary: Provides extensions to the PCE Communication Protocol to support the GMPLS control plane, addressing requirements identified in RFC 7025. This lets path computation work for Generalized MPLS networks, not only MPLS.

plainLanguage.summary: A GPS for network paths learns how to handle more kinds of roads, including optical ones, not just regular ones.

what is the pcep gmpls-capability tlv
what is the routing granularity flag in pcep
what is a generalized endpoint in pcep
subtitle: How PCEP is extended so path computation works for GMPLS networks such as optical transport, not only for MPLS.

tldr.problem: PCEP was written for MPLS networks, so it could not express what GMPLS path requests need: technology-specific bandwidth, unnumbered endpoints, label restrictions, protection attributes and the level of detail wanted in the returned route.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds new object types for BANDWIDTH, LOAD-BALANCING and END-POINTS, new TLVs for capability negotiation, labels and protection, a routing-granularity flag in the RP object, new NO-PATH-VECTOR bits and new error codes.
tldr.outcome: A PCC and PCE that both advertise the GMPLS-CAPABILITY TLV can use these extensions to compute paths for GMPLS TE-LSPs. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756.

facts.label: RG flag
facts.value: 2 bits, bits 15-16 of the RP object

today: RFC 8779 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted, so these extensions remain part of the PCEP specification for GMPLS.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needed GMPLS Extensions
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes paths for MPLS and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) networks. The architecture in RFC 4655 covers both, but the existing PCEP documents, such as RFC 5440 and RFC 5521, focus on MPLS and do not cover the wide range of GMPLS networks. Examples named here are Optical Transport Networks (OTNs) and Wavelength Switched Optical Networks (WSONs).

RFC 8779 complements those documents. It defines new object types, TLVs, encodings, error codes and procedures to meet the functional requirements listed in RFC 7025 and RFC 7449. The reader is expected to know those documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The old path-finding rules were written for ordinary roads. This document adds the extra words needed to ask for routes on more unusual networks, like ones made of light.

sections.title: Requirements and Gaps in Base PCEP
sections.content:
RFC 7025 groups the needs of GMPLS TE-LSPs into several categories: which data flow the LSP switches (switching type, encoding type, signal type), technology-specific traffic parameters such as concatenation, asymmetric bandwidth, unnumbered interfaces, technology-specific labels with label restrictions, and the requested granularity of the returned route (node, link or label).

Tables in the RFC check each requirement against what RFC 5440, RFC 5521 and RFC 8282 already provide. Switching, encoding and signal type are covered by the SWITCH-LAYER object, and the administrative group by LSPA. Most of the rest, including concatenation, end-to-end protection, asymmetric bandwidth and label constraints, is not supported.

The identified gaps are that BANDWIDTH and LOAD-BALANCING cannot describe GMPLS traffic details, END-POINTS cannot name unnumbered interfaces or label restrictions, IRO and XRO cannot include or exclude labels, and base attributes cannot express link or end-to-end protection.
sections.plainLanguage: First the authors checked a list of things a path request might need, then circled the ones the old rules could not say.

sections.title: Advertising and Negotiating GMPLS Capability
sections.content:
GMPLS-capable PCEs can be found through IGP-based PCE discovery, where bit 0 of the PCE-CAP-FLAGS sub-TLV means "Path computation with GMPLS link constraints" (RFC 5088 and RFC 5089). PCEs that set it MUST then qualify their support when a PCEP session is set up.

That is done with the new GMPLS-CAPABILITY TLV (type 45) in the OPEN object. A speaker able to support these extensions MUST include it in its Open message. If either peer leaves it out, the peers MUST NOT use the objects and TLVs from this document. If a speaker that supports the extensions, but did not advertise the capability, receives a message that uses them, it MUST send a PCErr with Error-Type 10 and Error-value 31 (Missing GMPLS-CAPABILITY TLV) and SHOULD end the session.

The TLV has a 32-bit Flags field. No flags are defined; unassigned flags MUST be zero on transmission and are ignored on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: Before two sides use the new vocabulary, each shows a badge saying it knows it. If one side has no badge, they stick to the old words.

sections.title: Granularity, Bandwidth and Load Balancing
sections.content:
A new 2-bit Routing Granularity (RG) flag, bits 15 and 16 of the RP object, lets the PCC say how much detail it wants in the returned ERO: node, link or label. Each level implies the ones before it, so label granularity means the ERO has node, link and label information. The PCE SHOULD follow the request and MAY return NO-PATH if it cannot. If it honors the request it MUST report the granularity it chose in the response; otherwise it uses the reserved value and the PCC checks the ERO itself.

The BANDWIDTH object gets two new object types: 3, Generalized bandwidth, and 4, Generalized bandwidth of an existing TE-LSP being reoptimized. They reuse the RSVP-TE traffic specification encodings, selected by a Bw Spec Type such as Intserv (2), SONET/SDH (4), G.709 (5), Ethernet (6), OTN-TDM (7) or SSON (8). An optional Reverse Generalized Bandwidth supports asymmetric requests; for symmetric ones the reverse length SHOULD be 0.

LOAD-BALANCING gains object type 2, Generalized Load Balancing, which carries Max-LSP and a minimum bandwidth spec for each member. Its meaning is unchanged: split the total bandwidth over at most Max-LSP TE-LSPs, each with at least the minimum. If the PCE cannot map the two bandwidth types, it MUST return NO-PATH with the bit "LOAD-BALANCING could not be performed with the bandwidth constraints". Appendix A shows an SDH example with 10 VC-4 containers split over paths of at least 2 VC-4 each.
sections.plainLanguage: You can now say how detailed the directions should be, and describe the size of your load in the units a particular kind of network really uses. You can also ask for it to be split across several routes.

sections.title: The Generalized Endpoint
sections.content:
END-POINTS gets object type 5, Generalized Endpoint. It allows endpoints of different types, unnumbered interfaces, and label restrictions on an endpoint. The object has an Endpoint Type field followed by TLVs. Type 0 is point-to-point; types 1 to 4 are point-to-multipoint with different leaf types, which a PCE may reject if it does not support P2MP computation, using Error-Type 4, Error-value 7.

The endpoint is given by an IPV4-ADDRESS (39), IPV6-ADDRESS (40) or UNNUMBERED-ENDPOINT (41) TLV. Optional restrictions are a LABEL-REQUEST TLV (42), which says the switching and encoding type, and LABEL-SET TLVs (43), which list allowed or preferred labels. A point-to-point request has exactly two endpoint TLVs, the source first and the destination second. In P2MP, the first is the root, which MUST be the same in all END-POINTS objects of one request.

LABEL-SET has three flag bits. U marks the upstream direction, O marks the old label in a reoptimization (which requires the R bit in the RP object), and L marks a loose, preferred set that the PCE MAY use. If the L bit is clear, the label allocated at the first endpoint MUST be inside the set. A PCE that cannot resolve an endpoint answers NO-PATH with "Unknown source" or "Unknown destination", and one that cannot meet a label restriction sets the "No endpoint label resource" or "No endpoint label resource in range" bit.
sections.plainLanguage: The start and end of a trip can now be described in more ways, and you can add notes such as only these lanes, please.

sections.title: Labels in IRO and XRO, and Protection in LSPA
sections.content:
The Include Route Object (IRO) and Exclude Route Object (XRO) can now carry a Label subobject (type 10), following the RSVP-TE ERO label encoding in RFC 3473. It MUST follow a subobject that identifies a link: an IP address (type 1 or 2) or an interface ID (type 4). More than one label subobject may follow a link. In the XRO, the X bit says whether the exclusion is mandatory (0) or only desired (1).

In the IRO, a PCE that can allocate labels MUST pick one from the listed values for the link. If it does not assign labels, it replies NO-PATH with the bit "No label resource in range".

The LSPA object may carry a new optional PROTECTION-ATTRIBUTE TLV (type 44), whose content comes from RFC 4872 and RFC 4873. The LSP flags and link flags can feed a PCE's routing policy, and the other attributes matter only to a stateful PCE. A PCE may ignore the TLV, and if it does, it MUST NOT include it in the response.
sections.plainLanguage: You can now say use this exact lane or avoid that lane, and also ask for a backup plan if the first road fails.

sections.title: NO-PATH Reasons and New Errors
sections.content:
The NO-PATH object is unchanged, but the NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV gains seven flag bits that explain a failure in GMPLS terms: bit 18 Protection Mismatch, 17 No Resource, 16 Granularity not supported, 15 No endpoint label resource, 14 No endpoint label resource in range, 13 No label resource in range, and 12 LOAD-BALANCING could not be performed with the bandwidth constraints.

New error values are added to Error-Types 4 (Not supported object) and 10 (Reception of an invalid object), and a new Error-Type 29, Path computation failure, is defined. The split is: Error-Type 29 reports constraints the PCE does not understand, for example a Generalized bandwidth it cannot interpret, while NO-PATH is used when the constraints are understood but cannot be satisfied.
sections.plainLanguage: When the answer is no route, the reply now says why: not enough room, wrong kind of backup, or the lane you asked for is not free.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
GMPLS LSPs can carry a high volume of traffic and be a critical part of a network, and the PCE helps decide their physical paths, so the identity of the PCE and PCC and the security of the channel matter. In many deployments the network is isolated, but where PCC-PCE communication is more exposed the RFC names three attacks. A malicious PCE posing as a real one can return paths through places where traffic can be sniffed, altered or dropped, or paths that quietly ignore requested constraints. A malicious PCC can learn the physical topology of critical infrastructure. Anyone able to inspect PCEP messages can also learn about the infrastructure.

PCE and PCC SHOULD use TLS as described in RFC 8253, which provides origin verification, message integrity and replay protection, and prevents third parties from reading messages. Against a malicious PCE, the PCC SHOULD have policies to accept or reject the returned path, checking that it follows the requested constraints. A technology-specific data-plane mechanism can also verify connectivity and deviations.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone pretends to be the map-maker, they could send you down a risky route or learn where the important roads are. So both sides prove who they are, keep their conversation private, and double-check the route.

fields.desc: No flags defined; zero on transmission, ignored on receipt.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Used by a PCE that did not honor the request; the PCC checks the ERO.

items.desc: ERO also includes labels, enabling explicit label control.
